title: Comments of the LPSC Staff on the NPO Motion for Subpoena for Production of Documents Issued by Deputy General Counsel Lauren T. Evans

documents.text:
BEFORE THE


                     LOUISIANA PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION


                              DOCKET NUMBER U-37882


                       ENTERGY LOUISIANA, LLC, EX PARTE.




  In re: Application of Entergy Louisiana, LLC for Certification of Generation and
     Transmission Resources and for Other Relief Pursuant to the Commission ’s

                                    Lightning Initiative

 COMMENTS OF THE LOUISIANA PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION STAFF
                       ON THE NPO MOTION FOR SUBPOENA
                         FOR PRODUCTION OF DOCUMENTS


         The Alliance for Affordable Energy and the Union of Concerned Scientists (jointly


“non—proﬁt organizations” or “NPOs”) ﬁled a Motion For Subpoena for the Production of

Documents pursuant to Rules 40 and 55 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the


Louisiana Public Service Commission          (“Commission”) on June 30, 2026 seeking the

issuance of a subpoena compelling the production of documents from Meta Platforms, Inc.


(“Meta”).    In accordance with the “Notice of Opportunity to File Response to        Subpoena

For the Production of Documents and Notice of Oral Argument” (“Notice”) issued by the



presiding Administrative Law Judge (“ALI”) on June 30, 2026, the staff of the Louisiana

Public    Service   Commission   (“Staff”)   submits   these   Comments   on   the   Motion   for


Subpoena.

         The NPO motion seeks production of documents from Meta, the parent company of



Evest, L.L.C., an Entergy Louisiana LLC (“ELL”) customer that is developing a large-


scale data center in Richland Parish, Louisiana adjacent to the data center currently under


construction by another Meta subsidiary, Laidley, LLC. ELL’s service to the Laidley data
 center was the     subject of LPSC Docket No. U-37425.                In this   docket, ELL is seeking


certiﬁcation of seven new generating units,         as   well   as   transmission and other assets in


connection with its service to Evest. ELL’s application seeks an unprecedented increase in


ELL’s load-serving resources and new investment of more than $14 billion dollars.


        The requested subpoena would order Meta to produce documents concerning (1)


economic    development expected to be caused by the data center; (2) the Customer’s

electric   load;   (3)   the   Customers’   load   factor   and      expected     load   variability;      (4)

communications between Meta and ELL discussing the Customer’s sustainability goals;


and (5) Meta’s assets and other guaranties Meta has made to other electric utilities.                   The


NPOs argue that all of the requested documents are essential to ELLs claims and that ELL


is not able to provide them because, to the extent they exist, they are in the possession of


Meta.   [NPO Motion at 4-5].

        As discussed in more detail below, there is precedent for the Commission’s issuance


of subpoenas to non-parties and to entities who are not regulated utilities, but Staff counsel


was   not able to find any cases where the         Commission directly addressed standards for


issuing a subpoena to a utility customer in a similar situation as Meta is here.               The NPOS


motion thus presents a largely      unprecedented question —to what extent the Commission

should compel the production of documents from              a   non-party utility customer seeking

service and doing business in Louisiana and who is the subject of the pending certification


application.   This question is presented in a case where the stakes are also unprecedented,




                                                                                         Docket No. U-37882
                                                                                                 P a g e    | 2
                                                            Staff’s Comments on NPO Motion for Subpoena
 with a request to certify billions of dollars of investment primarily to serve one customer,


set to be the largest customer in the state’s history.



         The Staff takes this   opportunity to comment generally on the Motion and the

signiﬁcant question it presents but will withhold taking a position on the speciﬁc requests

in the Motion until it has the opportunity to review any oppositions or other comments ﬁled


today.    The Staff will weigh in on the speciﬁc requests made in the Motion on the reply


deadline of July 7, 2026 as provided by the Notice.


I.       The Commission’s Subpoena Power Generally


         The Commission unquestionably has the power to subpoena documents and other


materials relevant to issues under its jurisdiction. The Louisiana Supreme Court has held


that, as to matters over which the Commission clearly has jurisdiction, its powers to issue

a    subpoena are generally co-extensive with judicial courts, and applicable throughout the

state of Louisiana. Standard Oil Co.   ofLouisiana v. Louisiana Pub. Serv. C0mm'n, 154 La.

557, 570, 97 So. 859, 864 (1923). General limiting principles on the scope of the court’s


subpoena power apply to the Commission.               See id.


          Rule 40 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure                        provides that the

Commission can issue “[s]ubpoenas for the             .   .   .   production of books, papers or documents

at a hearing in a pending proceeding    .   .   .
                                                    upon the written motion of a party showing that


there is good cause for the issuance of same.”                    Rule 40 requires that a party requesting a



subpoena must show that the documents requested will not impose “undue inconvenience




                                                                                               Docket No. U—37882
                                                                                                       P a g e | 3
                                                                      Staffs Comments on NPO Motion for Subpoena
 or   expense” on the party being subpoenaed and that the information being requested be

“relevant material and necessary.” It says:


               Motions for       subpoenas to compel the production of books,
               papers,    accounts       or    documents shall be veriﬁed and shall

               specify    as    nearly    as    may be    possible,      the    books, papers,
               accounts or documents desired and the material and relevant
               facts to be proved by them. No such subpoena shall be issued
               unless the  Secretary of the Commission shall determine that
               the matter sought is relevant material and necessary and that
               the production of such books, papers, accounts or documents
               will not result in unnecessary harassment, imposition, or undue
               inconvenience or expense to the party to be required to produce
               the same. No subpoena shall issue for material alleged to be of
               a    trade secret or conﬁdential nature unless it be shown after

               hearing of arguments on the same that no other alternative,
               such as a protective order, will accomplish a result consistent
               with the interests of all parties and the public.


LPSC Rule of Prac. & Proc. 40(B).               Thus, under Rule 40, the requested material must be


(1) relevant; (2) necessary; (3) not result in unnecessary harassment, imposition, or undue

inconvenience or expense; and (4) if the requested material is alleged to be “trade secret or


confidential,” then there must be a showing that no other alternative exists to accomplish

the sought result. Id.


        Rule   40    requires   these     determinations       to   be   made     by   the   Secretary   of the


Commission. However, Rule 55(0) of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure


delegates   to Administrative       Law        Judges   the   authority    to   “[i]ssue subpoenas       for the


                                                                                              99

production of documents and other evidence at depositions and hearings.                            Taking these

two rules   together, an Administrative Law Judge assigned to a docketed proceeding can




                                                                                              Docket No. U—37882
                                                                                                      P a g e l 4

                                                                    Staff s Comments on NPO Motion for Subpoena
 exercise their delegated authority to issue subpoenas subject to the same Rule 40 standards


that are applicable to the Commission Secretary in undocketed proceedings.


        Rule 40 further states that Commission can issue subpoenas for the “attendance or


witnesses from any place in the State ofLouisiana    .   .   .
                                                                 .”   (emphasis added). The locational

requirement for witnesses does not explicitly apply to documents under the terms of Rule

40.   And, in general, it appears that as long as an entity has sufficient contacts with the

State of Louisiana, it is subject to the subpoena power of the Commission.


        The Commission has previously issued subpoenas for the production of documents


to nonparty entities outside the state.   In Louisiana Public Service Commission v.            Bryant,

No.   T-33443, 2015 WL 1123062, at *5 (Mar. 10, 2015), for example, the Commission


instituted an investigation into Shelia Bryant dba VIP/Celebrity Limousine for an alleged


violation of the Charter Bus Order dated April 21, 1991, by providing interstate charter bus


service without registering with the Commission. Id. at *1. The Commission in that case


issued two subpoenas duces tecum to AT&T.


        Similarly, Administrative Law Judges have exercised their “delegated” authority to

issue subpoenas to nonparties and nonutilities in proceedings that are set for hearing before


the Commission.      See La. Pub. Serv. Comm ’n Rule 55(c).              In Entergy Louisiana, LLC v.


Southwest Louisiana Electric Membership Corporation (“SLEMCO ”) (LPSC Docket No.


U-35549), ELL filed a complaint alleging that SLEMCO violated the Commission’s 300-

foot rule by contracting to serve a developer of a new subdivision within ELL’s service


territory.   ELL sought documents and evidence in that proceeding through the submission



                                                                                      Docket No. U-37882

                                                                                              Pagel5
                                                             Staffs Comments on NPO Motion for Subpoena
 of motions to subpoena individuals associated with the Developer, including owners and


managers of the nonutility company that had contracted for service with ELL during earlier


phases of the development project.     The   presiding judge (Administrative Law Judge

Melanie Verzwyvelt) granted the motions and issued the subpoenas in that case pursuant


to her delegated authority.



       The same procedure for issuance of a subpoena was used in Entergy Louisiana, LLC



(LPSC Docket No. U-3 7425) when the NPOS ﬁled a motion to subpoena Meta in that case.

The presiding judge issued the subpoena there pursuant to her Rule 55 delegated authority.


Meta later moved to quash the subpoena. After oral argument, the presiding judge granted


Meta’s motion to    quash, but not because she did not have the authority to issue the

subpoena or because the NPOs had failed to satisfy their burden of proving that the

documents requested were relevant. Instead, she ruled that the NPOs’ request was untimely


because it “was made long after the agreed-upon May 9, 2025 deadline for discovery on


ELL’s direct   testimony and less than a month before the hearing.”          Ruling on Meta

Platforms, Inc.’s Motion to Quash Subpoena, Docket No. U-37425 (July 10, 2025).

       Louisiana courts have found that entities who are not citizens of Louisiana may be


considered residents of the state of Louisiana subject to the subpoena power of district


courts when those   entities have signiﬁcant contacts with the state. See,   e. g.,   LaBarre v.


Texas Brine Co., LLC, 2017-0309, pp. 12-13 (La. App. 1 Cir. 2/7/18), 347 So. 3d 949, 956-



57; EXCO Operating C0., LP 12. BRP, LLC, 56,018, pp. 7-8 (La. App. 2 Cir. 12/18/24), 402


So. 3d 668, 675 (ﬁnding that out-of-state corporations were residents of Louisiana subject



                                                                             Docket No. U-37882
                                                                                        P a g e   1 6
                                                     Staffs Comments on NPO Motion for Subpoena
 to the   subpoena power of a district court where they had signiﬁcant ties to the state,

including being registered to do business, maintaining a registered business establishment,

and doing business in Louisiana); Molaison v. Cust-0-Fab Specialty Servs., LLC, 21-585,



pp. 6-7 (La. App. 5 Cir. 6/1/22), 343 So. 3d 866, 871    (holding that a nonparty corporation

was a resident    of Louisiana subject to the state's subpoena power because the corporation


maintained    a   facility in Louisiana where the accident at issue occurred and employed

workers in that facility).


         Meta and Evest have significant contacts with the state to warrant a Commission-


ordered subpoena. Both are registered to do business in the state and have a registered agent


for service of process.      Meta and/or its subsidiaries own property in Richland Parish and


are   constructing two of the largest data centers in the world there.    Meta has committed to


invest millions of dollars in local infrastructure improvements and is actively hiring in the


state.   Meta’s Laidley data center is under construction,    as   are   the generating units and


transmission assets to serve that data center. Meta, Laidley and Evest have contracted with


ELL to become its biggest Louisiana customer.



         Taking the applicable rules and standards together, the Commission has the power

in general to issue a subpoena to Meta for documents and other materials and the presiding



judge has the delegated authority to issue that subpoena on findings that the subpoena

request complies with the requirements of Rule 40(B).




                                                                                 Docket No. U—37882
                                                                                         P a g e   | 7
                                                        Staffs Comments on NPO Motion for Subpoena
 II.        The Exercise of the Commission’s Subpoena Power to the NPOS’ Reguest


           Whether the NPOS’ subpoena request complies with the requirements of Rule 40(B)


is    a   fact-speciﬁc inquiry.     For every category of information           sought, the NPOs must

establish that the      information     is    (1) relevant; (2)    necessary;    (3)   will   not   result   in



unnecessary       harassment, imposition or undue inconvenience or expense; and (4) if the


requested material is alleged to be “trade secret or conﬁdential,” then that there is no other

alternative to obtain the         requested information.     The Staff would like to consider any


arguments and information presented in ELL’s opposition expected to be ﬁled today, as

well as in any other opposition or comments, before weighing in on whether these standards


are   met with respect the speciﬁc categories of documents sought.



           Strict scrutiny and careful consideration of whether those standards are satisﬁed are


particularly warranted here.         As a matter of public policy, the Commission should use its



subpoena power to obtain documents and other items from existing and prospective utility

customers       rarely, and only when such information is essential to a determination of a

necessary issue and is not available from the regulated utility or some other source.                    The


Commission should limit its subpoena reach to its jurisdictional utilities where possible to


avoid      subjecting other entities     to   undue   regulatory   burdens.     At the    same      time, the

Commission must take the actions necessary to ensure just and reasonable rates for all


utility customers.      Here, Meta and Evest have requested large-scale electric service in


Louisiana from a regulated utility, which has in turn ﬁled the instant application seeking




                                                                                         Docket No. U-37882

                                                                                                     Pagel8
                                                              Staff’ s Comments on NPO Motion for Subpoena
 certiﬁcation of billions of dollars of capital investment, at least some of which will be


recovered from ratepayers other than the Customer.


       It is appropriate for the Commission to subpoena relevant documents from Meta as



necessary to fulﬁll its regulatory obligations, but only after consideration of all evidence


and arguments and a strict application of the subpoena standards. The Staff appreciates the



opportunity to weigh in on the application of these standards to the NPOS’ request and will

do so on July 7, 2026 and at the oral argument on July 8, 2026, after evaluating the other


pleadings ﬁled today.




                                                Respectfully submitted,
